Once, the roof had been where the two of them hid cigarettes from the nuns. Now DOLORES and REMEDIOS pin sheets to the line, the wind off the estuary slapping them wet against their arms.
DOLORES: He asked me again from his bed this morning whether the boat was sold.
REMEDIOS: (a long pause, a clothespin in her teeth) And?
DOLORES: I said the buyer was still deciding. (She smooths a sheet that is already smooth.) Was that wrong?
REMEDIOS: You lied to a priest about a pear tree once. This is smaller.
DOLORES: (almost laughing) It isn't smaller.
REMEDIOS: No. (She lets the pin drop into the basket.) It isn't.
(They stand side by side. Below, a gull lands on the bakery chimney and folds its wings.)

items.passage: I was a terrible liar at eleven. Still, I told Matteo, the old man who sold me carp from a dented cooler at the edge of the salt flat, that my mother had sent me for the largest fish he had. She had not; I meant to bring it home and pretend I had caught it myself. Matteo looked at my coins, then at me, and wrapped the fish in newspaper without a word. I remember the white crust of salt cracking under my sandals as I walked back, the fish cold against my ribs, my chest bright with something like triumph. Years later the small ache of that lie still surprises me, but mostly I think of how carefully he folded the paper, tucking in the corners as if for a gift. Beyond his stall the flat shimmered all the way to the hills.

We had argued that morning over a cracked mirror, and for an hour we spoke only to customers. Then a woman lifted the carved sign from the bottom of a crate and read the name aloud. Yona looked at me, and I felt the old ease of being twins rush back, the way we used to finish each other's sentences at her table. Neither of us would sell it. We wrapped it in her red blanket and set it under the table, between our feet. By noon dust had settled on everything, and the vendor beside us was packing up his melons.

items.passage: I had soldered the same joint three times when Bogdan took the iron from my hand. 'Again,' he said, and set a cold radio in front of me. I wanted to tell him that no one fixes radios anymore, that I could be in Tel Aviv learning to code by now. Then I saw the folded letter under his ledger, an offer from a conservatory, dated forty years ago and never answered; my mother had told me he stayed to keep this shop open after my grandfather fell ill. Nobody sleeps in this room. SALMA, sixteen, sits beside RASHID, an old friend of her father's, under a buzzing light.
SALMA: The car was blue. I saw it.
RASHID: I saw gray. (He rubs his eyes.) But I was watching your father, not the road.
SALMA: The police will believe you. You're older.
RASHID: (turning the officer's notepad toward her) Then you write it. Your words, not mine.
(Salma hesitates, then writes. Rashid reads over her shoulder and, where she pauses, quietly tells her the date.)
SALMA: You're not going to change it?
RASHID: (shaking his head) Your father taught me to trust what a careful person sees.

items.passage: Radek tied the best knots in the building. items.passage: Bologna had flooded twice that spring, and the cellar still held a skin of brown water when Meera went down for the wedding linens. Her daughter followed with a torch. Near the stairs floated a paper crown, soft at the edges, its gold paint bleeding into the water. Meera lifted it out before her daughter could. Years ago, at six, the girl had made her promise to wear exactly that crown at the wedding, whoever the groom turned out to be. Upstairs, they spread the linens across chairs to dry and found every one of them ruined. The crown, pressed flat between two dictionaries, kept most of its shape. 'Marco will think we're mad,' her daughter said, but she was already testing it against her own hair. Rain began again on the courtyard tiles.

items.explanation: 종이 왕관은 딸이 여섯 살 때 결혼식에서 꼭 쓰겠다고 엄마와 약속한 물건이며, Meera는 딸보다 먼저 그것을 물에서 건져 낸다. 이후 결혼식 리넨은 모두 망가졌지만 왕관은 사전 사이에서 대부분 형태를 지키고, 딸은 그것을 자기 머리에 대어 본다. 두 단서를 이으면 왕관은 다른 것이 망가져도 남는 어린 시절의 유대를 상징하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 홍수 피해라는 문자적 의미에 머물렀고, B는 지문에 없는 두려움을, C는 딸의 행동과 반대되는 해석을 제시한다.

items.passage:
Smell of cut grass and the harbor's salt,
and a ball thudding off the far goalpost.
Okja sits on the bleacher's lowest step,
her mother's medicine in a paper bag.

The boys kick it high, past the chalk line,
past the fence, toward the road to Seoul,
and every time it bounces back,
fetched by someone smaller, running home.

She has packed a bag twice this year.
Twice she has unpacked it by morning.

When the ball rolls to her shoes at last,
she holds it for a while, feels its weight,
then tosses it gently back onto the field.
The floodlights blink on, one bank at a time,
and gulls drift low across the stands.
items.question: In the poem, the ball most likely represents which of the following?
options: Okja's urge to leave, which keeps bringing her back home
The carefree childhood that Okja wishes she could return to
The heavy burden of caring for a mother who needs medicine
The boys' dreams of escaping the city as famous players
items.explanation: 공은 서울로 가는 길 쪽으로 높이 차여 나가지만 매번 누군가에게 주워져 '집으로' 되돌아온다. 이어 Okja가 올해 두 번 가방을 쌌다가 아침이면 다시 풀었다는 연이 나오고, 마지막에 그녀는 공의 무게를 느낀 뒤 다시 경기장 안으로 던진다. 이 단서들을 이으면 공은 떠나고 싶지만 결국 어머니 곁으로 돌아오는 그녀의 마음을 상징하므로 A가 정답이다. B는 지문에 없는 그리움이고, C는 약봉지 소재를 빌렸지만 공과 연결되지 않으며, D는 소년들에 대한 해석이라 시의 초점과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Why does a man wear a hat indoors? My daughter, Priya, asked this of Mayor Marlon one wet afternoon in the drying shed of the tea estate above Surabaya, where I had come, as the town's only doctor, to discuss the fever in the pickers' quarters. Marlon laughed and tipped the wide straw brim lower. He told me the clinic would get its new beds after the harvest, the same promise he had made after the last harvest. Each time I pressed him on the numbers, he adjusted the hat, and its shadow slid across his eyes like a shutter. Later, walking down between the rows, Priya said she thought he must have been cold. I told her yes, perhaps. But I had noticed that when the estate owner arrived in his car, Marlon took the hat off at once and held it against his chest, his face suddenly bare and eager.
items.question: Based on the text, the mayor's hat most likely represents which of the following?
options: The authority Marlon holds over the pickers and the clinic
Marlon's habit of concealing himself from people he owes
The damp, chilly weather that fills the drying shed
Marlon's embarrassment at being questioned by a child
items.explanation: Marlon은 의사가 숫자를 따질 때마다 모자를 고쳐 써 그림자로 눈을 가리고, 약속은 매번 미뤄진다. 반면 농장주가 오자 즉시 모자를 벗고 맨얼굴을 드러낸다. 두 장면을 연결하면 모자는 자신에게 책임을 묻는 사람들 앞에서 자신을 숨기는 태도를 나타내므로 B가 정답이다. A는 권위를, C는 Priya의 순진한 해석을, D는 아이의 질문만을 근거로 한 오답이다.

items.passage: “He would have come, Yuying, if the river had let him,” Camryn says, and you do not believe him. The wedding hall is so crowded that the fiddlers must lean back against the wall, yet beside you one chair stands empty, a white card propped upon it bearing your father's name. You remember the letter from the conservatory in Memphis, the one that arrived the spring your father took the family savings downriver and did not return. Camryn had travelled with him that spring; you have always held him half to blame. Now he rests his hand upon the empty chair as he speaks, the way a man steadies himself against a rail. When the dancing begins and a cousin tries to borrow the chair, Camryn stops her gently. Leave it, he tells her. You notice that his own glass has stood untouched all evening, and that he will not look at the card.
items.question: Based on the text, the empty chair most likely symbolizes which of the following?
options: The narrator's lost chance to study at the conservatory
The crowding of the hall and the family's lack of money
An unresolved loss that weighs on Camryn as well as Yuying
Camryn's wish to take the father's place in the family
items.explanation: 빈 의자에는 떠나 돌아오지 않은 아버지의 이름표가 놓여 있고, Yuying은 그 일로 Camryn을 탓해 왔다. 그런데 Camryn은 의자에 기대듯 손을 얹고, 사촌이 의자를 가져가려 하자 막으며, 술잔도 건드리지 않은 채 이름표를 보지 못한다. 이 단서들을 이으면 의자는 두 사람 모두가 떨치지 못한 상실을 상징하므로 C가 정답이다. A는 아버지의 부재가 낳은 결과 하나만 본 것이고, B와 D는 지문의 근거가 없다.

items.passage: Three rules governed the old weaving house in Lisbon, and you learned them on your first day: no lamp after midnight, no cloth cut before it is finished, and no news spoken until it is certain. Rafaela, who had bought the house that winter, kept all three. Each morning she climbed to the loom room while Mateo, the gardener, pruned the lemon trees below, and each morning she wove one more row of a blue cloth with no pattern anyone could name. The ship carrying her brother was weeks overdue. When Mateo asked why she did not weave something useful, a shawl or a blanket, she only said that the cloth was not finished. Rows gathered like days. Once, when a rumor of a wreck came up the hill, her hands stopped above the threads for a full hour; then she tied the next knot and went on. By midsummer, Mateo had begun bringing her a sprig of lemon blossom each dawn and laying it, without a word, beside the growing blue.
items.question: Based on the text, the blue cloth most likely represents which of the following?
options: Rafaela's wish to make the old house useful again
The strict household rules that came with the house
The friendship slowly forming between Rafaela and Mateo
Rafaela's refusal to stop expecting her brother's return
items.explanation: Rafaela는 오빠의 배가 늦어지는 동안 매일 한 줄씩 천을 짜고, 끝나기 전에는 자르지 않는다는 규칙을 지킨다. 난파 소문에 한 시간 멈췄다가도 다시 매듭을 묶는 장면은 희망을 놓지 않는 태도를 보여 준다. 따라서 천은 오빠의 귀환을 계속 기다리는 마음을 상징하며 D가 정답이다. A는 Mateo의 제안을, B는 규칙 자체를, C는 마지막 장면의 꽃만을 근거로 한 그럴듯한 오답이다.

items.passage: Years later, Rangi would still remember the evening his son refused to leave the gymnasium in Lyon. It was the anniversary of Elodie's death, and Rangi had planned a quiet dinner at the restaurant she had loved. The boy, fourteen and immovable, had other ideas: he wanted to shoot free throws in the empty gym where his mother had once coached, one for every year since she had been gone. Rangi argued, then pleaded, then sat on the bottom bleacher with his coat still buttoned. His son did not answer. He simply kept shooting, building a wall of silence brick by brick with every bounce of the ball. Only on the fifth shot, when the ball rolled away toward the bleachers, did Rangi stand, pick it up, and pass it back.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “building a wall of silence brick by brick” most nearly suggests that the son
options: was damaging the gymnasium in his anger at his father
was growing too tired to keep arguing with his father
was shutting out his father's objections through steady repetition
was quietly showing off his skill to win his father's praise
items.explanation: 아들은 아버지의 설득과 애원에 대답하지 않고, 공을 튀길 때마다 침묵을 한 겹씩 더한다. '벽돌을 한 장씩 쌓는다'는 비유는 같은 동작의 반복으로 아버지의 반대를 차단하는 모습을 나타내므로 C가 정답이다. A는 벽을 문자 그대로 받아들인 해석이고, B와 D는 지문에 피로나 과시의 단서가 없다. 아버지가 결국 공을 건네주는 결말도 아들이 쌓은 벽을 아버지가 받아들였음을 보여 준다.

items.passage: Night is honest. In the sanatorium above the lake outside Bergen, I learned that patients say at two in the morning what they hide by daylight. Thorvald, my night patient, could not sleep unless I wheeled him to the end of the dock, where the water lay black and still. On the fourth night he showed me an envelope addressed to his brother, sealed and stamped and eleven years old. He had written it the week after their quarrel. He never mailed it, he said, and his brother had died the following spring. He held it on his blanket while he talked, and I understood that the apology had become an anchor he dragged behind him, slowing every hour he had left. Before dawn he asked me, Sigrid, to keep it for him. I put it in my apron pocket, where it weighed almost nothing.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “an anchor he dragged behind him” most nearly suggests that the unsent apology was
options: a source of steadiness that kept Thorvald calm at night
a memory Thorvald was ready to throw into the lake
a hope of reconciliation that still guided his choices
a weight of regret that kept holding Thorvald back
items.explanation: Thorvald는 형과 다툰 뒤 쓴 사과 편지를 11년 동안 부치지 못했고, 형은 이미 세상을 떠났다. 화자는 그 사과가 남은 시간을 늦추며 끌고 다니는 닻이 되었다고 말하는데, 이는 그를 붙잡는 후회의 무게를 뜻하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 닻의 '안정' 의미에 끌린 오답이고, B와 C는 형의 죽음으로 화해의 가능성이 사라졌다는 점과 맞지 않는다. 편지를 Sigrid에게 맡기자 거의 무게가 없었다는 대비도 이 해석을 뒷받침한다.

items.passage:
Who pays a clockmaker for the hours he gives away?
My father, Santiago, bent above his bench
on Forty-Third Street, where the trains shook dust
from the rafters into every open case.
Ottavio came in winter with a watch
his wife had worn, its mainspring broken, its glass
clouded like a frozen pond.
He counted out his nickels on the counter.
My father pushed them back without a word
and worked past closing, past supper, past the lamps,
spending his minutes like coins on a stranger
while I translated nothing, for nothing needed saying.
When the watch ticked, Ottavio wept in Italian.
My father answered him in Spanish.
I stood between them with my English,
the only one who thought words were required.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “spending his minutes like coins on a stranger” most nearly suggests that Santiago was
options: giving his own time freely in place of taking payment
wasting time carelessly on a repair he did not value
charging Ottavio for every minute of his labor
hurrying to finish the repair so he could close
items.explanation: Santiago는 Ottavio가 내민 동전을 말없이 돌려주고, 가게 문을 닫은 뒤에도 늦게까지 시계를 고친다. 그러므로 '분을 동전처럼 쓴다'는 비유는 돈 대신 자기 시간을 선물처럼 내어 주었다는 뜻이며 A가 정답이다. C는 동전이라는 단어에 끌린 오답이고, B와 D는 정성껏 오래 일한 장면과 어긋난다. 첫 행의 질문도 대가 없이 내어 준 시간이라는 주제를 미리 보여 준다.

### lit40-medium-01-027 — skill inferences · 유형 tone_or_mood
[지문]
Once, the roof had been where the two of them hid cigarettes from the nuns. Now DOLORES and REMEDIOS pin sheets to the line, the wind off the estuary slapping them wet against their arms.
DOLORES: He asked me again from his bed this morning whether the boat was sold.
REMEDIOS: (a long pause, a clothespin in her teeth) And?
DOLORES: I said the buyer was still deciding. (She smooths a sheet that is already smooth.) Was that wrong?
REMEDIOS: You lied to a priest about a pear tree once. This is smaller.
DOLORES: (almost laughing) It isn't smaller.
REMEDIOS: No. (She lets the pin drop into the basket.) It isn't.
(They stand side by side. Below, a gull lands on the bakery chimney and folds its wings.)

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall tone of the scene?
A) Playful teasing between old friends recalling childhood mischief
B) Wry amusement occasionally shadowed by brief flickers of doubt
C) Bitter resentment over a lie that one friend cannot forgive
D) Uneasy hesitation that is lightened now and then by wry humor

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
Dolores는 이미 매끈한 시트를 다시 펴고 '잘못한 걸까'라고 묻는 등 죽어 가는 친구에게 한 거짓말을 두고 불안하게 망설인다. 배 나무에 관한 거짓말 농담과 거의 웃을 뻔한 순간이 있지만, Remedios도 결국 '작은 일이 아니다'라고 인정하며 무거운 분위기로 돌아간다. 따라서 불안한 망설임에 가끔 씁쓸한 유머가 섞인 D가 정답이다. A는 덜 두드러진 유머만 말했고, B는 비중을 뒤집었으며, C는 지문에 단서가 없는 원망을 말한다.
### lit40-medium-01-028 — skill inferences · 유형 tone_or_mood

I was a terrible liar at eleven. Still, I told Matteo, the old man who sold me carp from a dented cooler at the edge of the salt flat, that my mother had sent me for the largest fish he had. She had not; I meant to bring it home and pretend I had caught it myself. Matteo looked at my coins, then at me, and wrapped the fish in newspaper without a word. I remember the white crust of salt cracking under my sandals as I walked back, the fish cold against my ribs, my chest bright with something like triumph. Years later the small ache of that lie still surprises me, but mostly I think of how carefully he folded the paper, tucking in the corners as if for a gift. Beyond his stall the flat shimmered all the way to the hills.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall tone of the passage?

B) Lasting guilt softened only slightly by moments of fondness

[해설]
화자는 소금 평원을 걸어 돌아오던 감각과 의기양양한 기분, 그리고 노인이 선물처럼 신문지를 접어 주던 모습을 애틋하게 회상한다. 거짓말의 작은 아픔이 아직 남아 있다고 하지만 '대부분'은 노인의 다정한 손길을 떠올린다고 말한다. 따라서 애틋한 향수에 희미한 죄책감이 섞인 A가 정답이다. B는 비중을 뒤집었고, C는 덜 두드러진 정서만 말했으며, D는 낯선 노인이라는 소재와 어울리지만 단서가 약하다.

Who else still remembered that our grandmother had called the house Two Ravens? Yona and I were selling what was left of it at the Saturday market, spreading her blankets and tin cups across a folding table in the wind. We had argued that morning over a cracked mirror, and for an hour we spoke only to customers. Then a woman lifted the carved sign from the bottom of a crate and read the name aloud. Yona looked at me, and I felt the old ease of being twins rush back, the way we used to finish each other's sentences at her table. Neither of us would sell it. We wrapped it in her red blanket and set it under the table, between our feet. By noon dust had settled on everything, and the vendor beside us was packing up his melons.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall mood of the passage?

B) Wistful affection that outlasts a brief strain between brothers

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]

By the time this reaches you, Abena, the cooperative will have finished sorting the dry-season seed. I have been given the cowpea jars, which you would find funny, since you once swore I could not tell one bean from another. Mother says you promised, before you left, that we would plant the back plot together when you came home. Neither of us can remember you saying it, and I worry a little that you will arrive and find that promise a stranger. Still, I have already set aside two jars with your name on them in my worst handwriting, and I keep picturing your hands in that red soil. Come soon. The jars are labeled. The neighbor's goats have learned to open our gate, so bring wire.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall tone of the letter?
A) Anxious uncertainty about whether the promise was ever made
B) Hesitant doubt relieved by only occasional moments of hope
C) Hopeful warmth that carries a slight trace of uncertainty
D) Dutiful formality suited to reporting on the cooperative

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
Efua는 기억나지 않는 약속을 Abena가 낯설게 여길까 '조금' 걱정한다고 쓰지만, 곧바로 이름을 적은 씨앗 병 두 개를 따로 두었고 붉은 흙 속의 손을 그려 본다고 말한다. '빨리 와'라는 말과 장난스러운 농담까지 더해져 따뜻한 기대감이 지문을 이끈다. 따라서 희망찬 따뜻함에 약간의 불확실함이 섞인 C가 정답이다. A는 덜 두드러진 정서만, B는 비중을 뒤집은 정서를 말하며, D는 협동조합 보고라는 소재와 어울리지만 격식 있는 어조의 단서가 없다.
### lit40-medium-01-031 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters

I had soldered the same joint three times when Bogdan took the iron from my hand. 'Again,' he said, and set a cold radio in front of me. I wanted to tell him that no one fixes radios anymore, that I could be in Tel Aviv learning to code by now. Then I saw the folded letter under his ledger, an offer from a conservatory, dated forty years ago and never answered; my mother had told me he stayed to keep this shop open after my grandfather fell ill. I picked up the iron without arguing. When he leaned over to check my work, I tilted the lamp toward his side so he would not have to squint. Outside, a bus groaned up the hill toward the port.

[질문] Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Tamar and Bogdan?
A) Tamar feels only frustration with an elder who refuses to modernize.
B) Bogdan feels indebted to Tamar's family for the sacrifices they made.
C) Bogdan is a stern master who treats Tamar as a mere hired hand.

Years later, Rangi would still remember the evening his son refused to leave the gymnasium in Lyon. It was the anniversary of Elodie's death, and Rangi had planned a quiet dinner at the restaurant she had loved. The boy, fourteen and immovable, had other ideas: he wanted to shoot free throws in the empty gym where his mother had once coached, one for every year since she had been gone. Rangi argued, then pleaded, then sat on the bottom bleacher with his coat still buttoned. His son did not answer. He simply kept shooting, building a wall of silence brick by brick with every bounce of the ball. Only on the fifth shot, when the ball rolled away toward the bleachers, did Rangi stand, pick it up, and pass it back.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “building a wall of silence brick by brick” most nearly suggests that the son
A) was damaging the gymnasium in his anger at his father
B) was growing too tired to keep arguing with his father
C) was shutting out his father's objections through steady repetition
D) was quietly showing off his skill to win his father's praise

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
아들은 아버지의 설득과 애원에 대답하지 않고, 공을 튀길 때마다 침묵을 한 겹씩 더한다. '벽돌을 한 장씩 쌓는다'는 비유는 같은 동작의 반복으로 아버지의 반대를 차단하는 모습을 나타내므로 C가 정답이다. A는 벽을 문자 그대로 받아들인 해석이고, B와 D는 지문에 피로나 과시의 단서가 없다. 아버지가 결국 공을 건네주는 결말도 아들이 쌓은 벽을 아버지가 받아들였음을 보여 준다.
### lit40-medium-01-045 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
Night is honest. In the sanatorium above the lake outside Bergen, I learned that patients say at two in the morning what they hide by daylight. Thorvald, my night patient, could not sleep unless I wheeled him to the end of the dock, where the water lay black and still. On the fourth night he showed me an envelope addressed to his brother, sealed and stamped and eleven years old. He had written it the week after their quarrel. He never mailed it, he said, and his brother had died the following spring. He held it on his blanket while he talked, and I understood that the apology had become an anchor he dragged behind him, slowing every hour he had left. Before dawn he asked me, Sigrid, to keep it for him. I put it in my apron pocket, where it weighed almost nothing.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “an anchor he dragged behind him” most nearly suggests that the unsent apology was
A) a source of steadiness that kept Thorvald calm at night
B) a memory Thorvald was ready to throw into the lake
C) a hope of reconciliation that still guided his choices
D) a weight of regret that kept holding Thorvald back

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
Thorvald는 형과 다툰 뒤 쓴 사과 편지를 11년 동안 부치지 못했고, 형은 이미 세상을 떠났다. 화자는 그 사과가 남은 시간을 늦추며 끌고 다니는 닻이 되었다고 말하는데, 이는 그를 붙잡는 후회의 무게를 뜻하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 닻의 '안정' 의미에 끌린 오답이고, B와 C는 형의 죽음으로 화해의 가능성이 사라졌다는 점과 맞지 않는다. 편지를 Sigrid에게 맡기자 거의 무게가 없었다는 대비도 이 해석을 뒷받침한다.
### lit40-medium-01-046 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language
[지문]
Who pays a clockmaker for the hours he gives away?
My father, Santiago, bent above his bench
on Forty-Third Street, where the trains shook dust
from the rafters into every open case.
Ottavio came in winter with a watch
his wife had worn, its mainspring broken, its glass
clouded like a frozen pond.
He counted out his nickels on the counter.
My father pushed them back without a word
and worked past closing, past supper, past the lamps,
spending his minutes like coins on a stranger
while I translated nothing, for nothing needed saying.
When the watch ticked, Ottavio wept in Italian.
My father answered him in Spanish.
I stood between them with my English,
the only one who thought words were required.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “spending his minutes like coins on a stranger” most nearly suggests that Santiago was
A) giving his own time freely in place of taking payment
B) wasting time carelessly on a repair he did not value
C) charging Ottavio for every minute of his labor
D) hurrying to finish the repair so he could close

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
Santiago는 Ottavio가 내민 동전을 말없이 돌려주고, 가게 문을 닫은 뒤에도 늦게까지 시계를 고친다. 그러므로 '분을 동전처럼 쓴다'는 비유는 돈 대신 자기 시간을 선물처럼 내어 주었다는 뜻이며 A가 정답이다. C는 동전이라는 단어에 끌린 오답이고, B와 D는 정성껏 오래 일한 장면과 어긋난다. 첫 행의 질문도 대가 없이 내어 준 시간이라는 주제를 미리 보여 준다.
